carousels.name: Holiday trips home are a p*rn relapse risk

slides.title: Going home for the holidays? [[Your childhood bedroom is a p*rn relapse trap.]]
slides.sub: Old room, old habits. Plan ahead.

slides.title: Old [[cues]]
slides.body: Same bed, same desk, same door you used to lock. Your brain remembers what happened there. Many guys say the urge to watch p*rn hits the moment they walk in.

slides.title: Family [[stress]]
slides.body: Arguments, old roles, questions about your job or love life. Stress at home has to go somewhere. Don't let it go to p*rn.

slides.title: Lots of [[idle]] time
slides.body: Long afternoons, late nights, nothing scheduled. Boredom plus privacy is the classic setup.

slides.title: Your trip [[plan]]
items: Rearrange the room a little on day one.
Leave the door open when you're on your laptop.
Plan daily outings — gym, walks, old friends.
Text your accountability partner every night.

carousels.name: Should you tell people you're doing NNN?

slides.title: Day 19: should you tell people you're quitting p*rn [[— or keep it private?]]
Tell [[people]]
slides.body: Saying it out loud makes it real. Friends can check in. You're less likely to cave on p*rn when someone will ask.

slides.title: Keep it [[private]]
slides.body: Announcing goals can feel like progress — without doing the work. And jokes from friends can make it harder.

slides.title: Our [[take]]
slides.body: Don't announce it to everyone. Tell one or two people who'll actually support you. Small circle, real accountability, no performance.

Someone you talk to most days.
Someone who'd notice if you went quiet.

carousels.name: 5 questions researchers use to spot problematic p*rn use

slides.title: Depending on the test, 3.2% to 16.6% of people [[are at risk of problematic p*rn use.]]
slides.sub: Here are the kinds of questions those tests ask.

slides.title: At [[risk]]
slides.body: The International Sex Survey (Bőthe et al., 2024) found 3.2%–16.6% of people were at risk, depending on the measure — with men reporting the highest levels.

slides.title: Questions [[1–3]]
items: Do you feel you need more p*rn to get the same effect?
Have you tried to cut back and failed?
Do you use p*rn to deal with stress or bad moods?

slides.title: Questions [[4–5]]

Do you feel restless or irritable when you can't watch it?

slides.title: Said yes to [[several]]?

carousels.name: The scan: why you can't stop checking women out

slides.title: Can't stop "scanning" every woman you pass? [[P*rn trained that reflex.]]
slides.sub: And women notice it more than you think.

slides.title: The [[scan]]
slides.body: Eyes go straight to bodies — on the street, at the gym, in meetings. Years of p*rn trains your attention to hunt.

slides.title: Women [[feel]] it
slides.body: Being scanned feels like being treated as a body, not a person. Many women say they notice it instantly — and remember it.

slides.title: It can be [[retrained]]
slides.body: Attention is a habit. Habits can change. Many men say the reflex faded after time away from p*rn.

Look at faces — eyes, expressions, people.
Bounce your eyes away and keep walking.

slides.body: If you can stay up till 2 AM scrolling p*rn, the energy is there. What's missing is the decision.

slides.title: Easy vs. [[effort]]
slides.body: P*rn asks nothing from you. Training, building, calling someone — they ask for effort. Your brain picks easy every time unless you decide first.
